chapter_theme: Akananuru 81 to 100 in the anthology's fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems of men crossing the waste for wealth, of their return, and of a girl's elopement seen by her foster mother and by her lover; hill courtships under watch and a veriyattu rite; marutham marriage and infidelity, from a wedding night remembered to gossip loud as a Chola victory; mullai war camps and homecomings; and neythal confinement and pressure for marriage. Kings and towns of puram (Pulli's Venkatam, Kuttuvan's Kudanadu, Uraiyur, Koodal, Karuvur, Paruvur, Viyalur, Puranthai) serve as measures of distance, wealth and noise.

81.reading: The friend, having read the woman's heart, asks the man who has announced his going whether he will really cross the long burning waste for wealth made by going away, where a bear tired of sweet iruppai fruit digs out a termite mound and a kite pines alone on a sun-scorched maraa tree, while her lovely kohl-dark eyes, fair as Kadalan's town Vilangil, run with tears.
81.nuance: The question is put in the plural of respect (ஐய! சேறிரோ) and closes on the wealth itself, அகன்றுசெய் பொருள், wealth that is made by leaving: the friend names the price inside the word for the prize. The bear that turns from sweet fruit when it is sated to dig in a hard mound for a meal could be read as the man who leaves a sweet home for hard-won wealth, but the poem draws no pairing, so it is left as scene.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவுணர்த்திய தலைமகற்குத் தோழி தலைமகள் குறிப்பறிந்து வந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the summer waste where the earth cracks is the road he means to take

comparisons.tenor: the bear's snout blowing as it digs the mound, like a bellows nozzle
her kohl-dark lovely eyes, as fair as Kadalan's town

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the friend speaks for the woman, having read her mind (குறிப்பறிந்து)

82.reading: The woman tells her friend that the hill man's country is a stage where wind in bored bamboo is the flute, the waterfall the drum, the stag's call the horn and the bees the lute, the monkeys an amazed audience and the peacock a dancer; many saw him standing at the gap of the millet field with his bow, asking after the elephant he had hunted, so why should she alone lie through the dark night with streaming eyes and slackened arms?
82.nuance: Telling the friend this is the first step of disclosure (அறத்தொடு நிற்றல்): she admits she met him, but in the form of a complaint that many saw him and only she suffers. The hill's whole orchestra plays to an audience of monkeys, and the one hearer it truly moves is she, alone at night.

colophon.thurai: தோழிக்குத் தலைவி அறத்தொடு நின்றது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill slope, the millet field and the hunter with bow fix the hill land

comparisons.tenor: the west wind in the bored bamboo, as a flute
the waterfall's sound, as a drum
the humming bees, as a lute
the female monkeys, as the assembly watching a performance
the dancing peacock, like a dancer entering the stage

83.reading: On the road, the man tells his heart that though he has passed the Venkatam hill of Pulli, chief of the unlettered young men who wear maraa flowers, tear an elephant calf from its wailing mother and tie it at the toddy-houses of their flag-lined town in exchange for drink, his love's virtues, her rain-moist eyes like an opening neythal flower, did not count the distance and have come all the way to reach him.
83.nuance: Paalai usually makes the woman the one whom memory reaches; here her qualities (குணனே) are the travellers, driven by love (அன்புமிகக் கடைஇ) across the frontier he has just crossed. The cow elephant crying in the forest for the calf the young men have taken sits behind his thought of the woman he left, but the poem does not draw the pairing.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்துத் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: he has gone far from her beyond the frontier hill and is still on the road

comparisons.tenor: her lovely rain-moist eyes

84.reading: In the war camp the man says that the rains have come, a rainbow on the hill and drum-voiced clouds pouring till the directions vanish, and she of the bright brow is in her small village on the frontier woodland where mullai flowers drop on a sleeping boar's back; while he is in the camp of a garlanded king who, angry, will not accept even the rare tribute of a fortress set among rich fields of reapers and toddy-drinking labourers, and moves his army on to fight.
84.nuance: Two lands face each other across the poem: her mullai woodland in the promised rains, and the enemy's marutham fields where the harvest goes on. The rains that should send him home have come; what keeps him is the king's anger, which turns down the very tribute that would end the war (அருந்திறை கொடுப்பவும் கொள்ளான்).

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பாசறை இருந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the rains have come over her mullai woodland while he is held at war

comparisons.tenor: the boar's small red eyes
the many red flowers of the fields, like fire

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named: he speaks his thought in the camp

85.reading: The friend tells the woman not to weep in reproach that the man who left them is without virtue while her brow pales and her arms waste: he assured them he would come back in the cool rains, when on the slopes of Thiraiyan's tall Venkatam hill the bull elephant breaks young bamboo shoots to feed the hungry calf of his soft-stepping mate, and the peacock, bathed in vengai pollen, calls its mate from the kurunthu branch; that is the season, and the rain has spread.
85.nuance: The comfort is built from his own words: the friend quotes the promise, scene and all, and then points to the sky. The elephant feeding his mate's calf is inside that promise, so the man himself had chosen the image of a male who provides.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பிரிய வேறுபட்ட தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறுத்தியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the heart of the poem is waiting for a return promised for the rains, which is mullai's situation

iraicchi.act: the bull elephant breaks young bamboo shoots and feeds them to the hungry calf of his mate, who has lately given birth
iraicchi.sense: the man who named this scene in his promise is one who provides for his own, so his word to return can be trusted

86.reading: The man recalls the wedding: rice cooked with black gram heaped high, sand spread under the cool pandal, lamps and garlands, the auspicious dawn when the moon stood free of the evil planet; matrons with pots and bowls passing things in order; four mothers of sons pouring water with petals and paddy on her hair and blessing her never to fail in chastity and to love the man who took her; her kin then giving her as lady of the great house; and the first night, when she lay curled in her new cloth with her face hidden, and asked what her heart felt, she only bowed her head in deep joy.
86.nuance: The blessing (கற்பினின் வழாஅ, நற்பல உதவிப் பெற்றோற் பெட்கும் பிணையை ஆக) is the karpu ideal spoken by women who have kept it. By the colophon's first reading the man tells all this to the friend who has shut the door on him, so the memory of the wedding becomes his plea against a quarrel the poem never names. Her answer to his question is a gesture, not a word.

colophon.thurai: வாயில் மறுத்த தோழிக்கு தலைமகன் சொல்லியது தலைமகளைக் கூடி இன்புற்றிருந்த தலைமகன் பண்டு நிகழ்ந்தது சொற்று இன்புற்றிருந்ததூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is a household wedding with no landscape; its situation is union, and the marutham placement rests on the colophon's door refused

comparisons.tenor: her shy, wondering glance, as a deer's

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: with his wife, recalling the first night

87.reading: Coming home with his work done, the man tells his heart that it suffered long on the road, lodging for the night in a poor hamlet of grass huts where a calf sucks the churning stick hung in the yard, leaving at the cock's first call, and passing hill forks where the drum of fierce marauders from their rock forts makes travellers' hearts quake; now let it rejoice, for they will praise her breasts and lie in her bamboo-smooth arms in their tall house where the lamp burns all night.
87.nuance: The hamlet's small homely detail, a calf mouthing the curd-stick under a creeper pandal, is the first sight of a home on the way back and foreshadows his own; the heart, not the man, is the traveller who suffered (நனிநீடு உழந்தனை).

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீளுந் தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்துத் தன் நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem looks back on the waste road of marauders he has crossed

comparisons.tenor: her arms, smooth and long as bamboo

88.reading: With the man listening outside, the friend wonders whether the good man who came guided by the torch a hunter had set on his platform to watch for the boar stealing to the red millet, and who ended their trembling grief, has gone back by that path no one can tread, where a tiger-killing elephant's musth draws bees whose hum the asunam takes for a lute, where snakes crowd the bamboo thicket and the bear digs at deep anthills.
88.nuance: The catalogue of dangers is spoken for the listener outside: a road this perilous cannot be walked every night, and only marriage ends the need. The torch set to catch a thief is the light the lover came by.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: millet field, hunter and hill fix the land

comparisons.tenor: the bees' hum at the musth, taken by the asunam for a lute

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: she speaks to the woman (நம் நடுங்குதுயர்) for the man standing by

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the boar and millet of the hill field, a thing of the poem's own land (porul 7.27)

89.reading: The foster mother, after the girl has gone off with her man, asks whether she can walk on her soft red feet across the wide burning land where the rains failed and the mirage runs, where the owl booms like struck stone in the crevices, cicadas shrill in the thorn trees, and marauders who have eaten pale meat cut down the guards of a donkey caravan and share out the loot to the beat of the drum, she who would not drink honeyed milk even when coaxed and played under the sand-strewn pandal.
89.nuance: The road is all violence and the man does not appear at all: the mother can only measure the girl's feet against the land. The last lines bring the reader back into the house, to the milk she refused and the pandal where she played, so the loss is set in the very place the girl has left.

colophon.thurai: மகட்போக்கிய செவிலித்தாய் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a girl gone off with her lover through the waste, grieved by the mother left behind

comparisons.tenor: the owl's booming cry

90.reading: The friend meets the man leaving after a day tryst on the shore where white-crested waves like old men wreck the sand houses of the young girls, and tells him that gossip of their union, known to few, has risen and the girl has been shut up at home; she cannot tell him to go away while he suffers so, but her people would not take even the rich market of the dark-eyed Kosar east of Chellur as enough for her.
90.nuance: The waves likened to old men (மூத்தோர் அன்ன) that break the play-houses of the young are the elders who have shut the girl in and broken off the lovers' meetings, and the friend never says so. The closing bride-price line turns on பாசிலை, whose sense here (a green leaf of a courtship gift, or her worth) the text does not settle.

colophon.thurai: பகற்குறி வந்து கண்ணுற்று நீங்கும் தலைமகனைத் தோழி எதிர்ப்பட்டு நின்று இற்செறிப்பு அறிவுறீஇயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the waves, the screwpine grove and the shore ford fix the seashore

comparisons.tenor: the white-crested waves
the Kosar market's noise, as the roar of the sea

ullurai.tenor: the girl's elders, who have shut her in and ended the meetings

pairs.situation: the old ones of her house
they break up the young lovers' play of meeting

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the waves of their own shore, without leaving the land (porul 7.27)

91.reading: The friend tells the wasting woman that though the man left for rare wealth across a waste where the sun has dried the falls, and an elephant that found no water in the dread pool ate moss and shrank together with his hungry mate, he has great love: even if he gained Kuttuvan's Kudanadu beyond the marauders' scrub, a land of drums that knows no hunger, where the buffalo tired of lotus rests in the shade of old jackfruit trees, he would not stay there forgetting her beauty.
91.nuance: The wealth the man went for is measured by the richest land the friend can name, and the claim is that he would refuse it. The elephant pair is on his road, the buffalo in the land he would refuse.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை மெலிந்த தலைமகளைத் தோழி வற்புறுத்தியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the falls have dried and the wide land shimmers in the heat

iraicchi.act: finding no water, the elephant eats moss and shrinks together with his hungry mate
iraicchi.sense: even beasts in the drought keep together, so the man who crossed that land has not stopped loving her

92.reading: The friend tells the man not to come on such nights, when lightning blinds the slopes and in the pouring midnight rain a striped tiger strikes an elephant and roars; tomorrow she and the girl will be guarding millet, and in a grove so thick that not even the monkeys know it, by a cool fall where red kanthal has opened, he may have the sleep of her soft dark hair, by the light of a gem from a snake that thunder has struck.
92.nuance: The day tryst she offers is made of impossibilities, a grove unknown to monkeys and a lamp from a thunder-killed snake's gem, so that the man hears what the colophon says she means: marriage, not meetings (வரைவு கடாயது).

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிச் சென்று தலைமகளைக் கண்ணுற்று நீங்குத் தலைமகனைப் பகற்குறி நேர்ந்த வாய்பாட்டால் தோழி வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: millet guarding and the kanthal by the fall fix the hill

comparisons.tenor: the snake's gem, as a lamp

93.reading: Coming home with his work done, the man tells his heart: to end the kin's ruin, feed the relatives and make friends of strangers, he went with zeal for effort and won rare treasure as fine as the just assembly of the Cholas at Uraiyur; now let them go and embrace, more times than the sands heaped on the banks of the Porunai at Kothai's Karuvur, the dark woman whose brow smells like the morning market of Vazhuthi's Koodal, in their sky-high house on a bed soft as gathered foam by the tall lamp, till her ornaments print their marks on her.
93.nuance: The opening gives the paalai journey a household reason: wealth is for the kin, the relatives and the stranger made friend. The three crowned houses each lend one simile: the Chola court for wealth, the Pandya market for her scent, the Chera river's sands for the count of embraces.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீளலுறுந் தலைமகன் இடைச்சுரத்துத் தன்னெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is the return from a parting for wealth

comparisons.tenor: the rare treasure he has won
her fragrant brow
their tall house, as if carved from a mountain
the soft flower bed, like gathered foam
the number of their embraces

94.reading: Returning, the man tells his charioteer that her town, the town of the woman of thick dark hair and loving gentleness, lies in the hard woodland country where at midnight the musundai blooms white like the sky, a goatherd with a leather bag, wearing a dripping garland of mullai and thondri, warms his palms at a sputtering brand and whistles long into the dark where the jackal howls, together with the black horn the field-guards blow to drive off herds of boar.
94.nuance: Her town is reached through its night sounds, the herdsman's whistle and the guards' horn, heard as one; the herdsman out in the dark, warming his hands far from home, is a figure of the man himself.

colophon.thurai: வினைமுற்றி மீளுந் தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது தலைமகன் பாங்கற்குச் சொற்றதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the herdsman, the mullai garland and the woodland country

comparisons.tenor: the musundai's white flowers, as the starry sky

95.reading: The woman tells her friend that her brow has paled, her leaf-tender body thinned and her grief shows for all to see, and thinking can end it only with her life; the town, fond of gossip, will not say she grieves for one who crossed the wastes where a bear and her cubs carry off the hail-like iruppai flowers, and her mother has answered the women of the town that their harsh words do not fit her daughter: before such a mother, who understands and is calm, what can she do in this state?
95.nuance: The mother here does not scold; she defends the girl against the town, and that is what the girl cannot bear, since the mother's trust is what she is about to betray. The colophon says the speaker is தலைமகன், but the poem's first person is the woman (என் தளிர்புரை மேனி, என் மகட்கு in the mother's mouth).

colophon.thurai: போக்குடன் பட்ட தலைமகன் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the iruppai and the bear of the wastes he crossed

comparisons.tenor: her body, tender as young leaves
the hollow iruppai flowers, like hailstones

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon reads தலைமகன் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது, but the speaker is plainly the woman; see source_issues

96.reading: The friend, refusing the man entry, calls him lord of a kaanji town where in the field-pond prawns leap like a bow sprung loose, and a thorny cane, its long stem toothed like a file, catches the broad leaves of the water lily and, swung by the north wind, swells and slackens like a forge's bellows; they say he has chosen one young girl out of all the bangled band, and that news has spread through many mouths like the uproar of elephants taken on the day the Chola, father of Aqthai, beat both great kings on the battlefield of Paruvur.
96.nuance: The friend matches his private conquest to a royal victory's din: what he thought hidden is as public as a war. The cane that catches the lily and swells and slackens with every wind is his way with women.

colophon.thurai: தோழி வாயின் மறுத்தது

thinai_evidence.note: field pond, paddy land and kaanji town

the cane's thorny stem

the gossip of his new girl

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the young girl he has taken

pairs.situation: he catches and holds the new girl
his desire swells and slackens with each new attraction

97.reading: The woman answers her friend, who tells her not to weep thinking of the cruel man who crossed a waste where the spotted stag's horns fall in the drought and vultures and kites gather at a stench the tiger left, like marauders cutting up meat in rock clefts after a night raid on cattle: how can she easily stop her tears, hearing the sated koel call in spring, when the kuravam blooms, the cold season is over, marutham trees crowd the river ford and new mango flowers crown the boughs under smoky mist?
97.nuance: The friend's comfort carries a compliment (her bosom fair as Nannan's Viyalur, a court that cherished bards), and the answer sets against it the joy of spring: the koel is நுகர்குயில், a bird that has had its fill, and it is the season's plenty, not the waste, that makes tears impossible to stop.

colophon.thurai: வற்புறுந்துந் தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: she weeps for the man gone across the waste

comparisons.tenor: the vultures and kites crowding at the carrion
her bloomed bosom
the mist creeping over the mango boughs

98.reading: With the man standing by, the girl tells her friend that her mother does not know the ache of his withheld grace can be eased only on his chest; seeing her bangles slip, the mother asked the old lying women, who said it was Murugan's seizure, and so a velan dances in the decorated pandal to restore her beauty: if after all that her wasted body does not recover the secret will become gossip, and worse, if the god relieves her and the hill man hears that her sickness was something else, living will be harder still.
98.nuance: The rite is described with care and mocked in the same breath (மையற் பெண்டிற்க்கு நொவ்வல்): the women are deluded, the velan dangles like a puppet. Her deepest fear is not exposure but that the rite might work, and the man conclude she never pined for him.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்ச் சொல்லியது. தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொல்லிய தூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill lord and Murugan's rite fix the hill land

comparisons.tenor: the well-made house, like a painting
her admired beauty, like a doll's
the velan dangling in his dance

99.reading: Leading the girl who has gone off with him, the man coaxes her to look at the forest, strewn with palasa buds red as a tiger's claws, kongam opening like jewelled breasts, athiral and paathiri petals and maraa blossoms, lovely as the flower-strewn town of a dread god, and asks whether it also has hills of all heights that look like her father's war elephants, tusk-rings broken, crowded by their mates.
99.nuance: This is the same kind of road that the foster mother of 89 fills with marauders; the lover makes it a temple town of flowers. His last question teases and reassures at once: even the hills are her father's elephants, so she has not left home behind.

colophon.thurai: உடன் போகிய தலைமகளைத் தலைமகன் மருட்டிச் சொல்லியது,

thinai_evidence.note: he leads a girl away from her father's house through the forest

100.reading: The friend tells the man that it is sweet to her too that he comes, wipes off his sandal, embraces the girl till her breast is marked, and leaves in the dark; but the gossip has come true, loud as a newly arrived flock of storks at the punnai-grove ford of Puranthai, town of the bards' patron Periyan, where fishers' lamps on the stilled sea at night shine like the face-lamps of a king's dancing war elephants; theirs is a sorrowing town of screwpine gardens where the buffalo that went out at cold dawn feeds on fresh neythal flowers.
100.nuance: Line 4 is irony: what is sweet to the friend is exactly what she is ending. The buffalo that goes out at dawn and grazes the fresh neythal flower of their own town is the man who takes the girl's youth and leaves before light.

colophon.thurai: தோழி வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai shore grove, screwpine and fishing fix the seashore

comparisons.tenor: the fishers' bright lamps on the night sea
the gossip

ullurai.tenor: the lover who takes the girl's fresh youth by night and is gone before light

pairs.situation: he leaves while it is still dark
he enjoys the young girl of this shore

ullurai.speaker_fit: the friend uses the buffalo grazing in their own town's gardens, without leaving the poem's land (porul 7.27)

links.note: Both name Pulli's Venkatam: in 61 the friend says the man would not stay even for Venkatam with its festivals; in 83 the man says her virtues followed him past Venkatam regardless of distance.
links.teaches: Pulli's Venkatam served akam poets as the fixed far edge of the wealth journey, and they turned it both ways: a prize too small to hold the man, and a distance too short to stop the woman's pull.

links.note: Venkatam is Thiraiyan's hill of the victorious spear in 85 and lies in the land of Pulli, chief of the unlettered young men, in 83.
links.teaches: The same frontier hill is credited to two different lords by poets of one anthology, so Venkatam in akam is a border claimed by more than one chief, not a fixed realm.

links.note: In 44 the enemies pay their tribute and the man drives home; in 84 the king refuses the tribute offered and the man stays in the camp through the promised rains.
links.teaches: The mullai homecoming hangs on one puram act, the king's acceptance of tribute: taken, it frees the soldier, refused in anger, it holds him, so the woman's waiting is timed by a royal decision she never sees.

links.note: The foster mother in 89 sees the elopement road as a waste of marauders, slaughtered guards and failed rains; the lover in 99 calls the same kind of forest good and lovely, a temple town strewn with flowers.
links.teaches: The anthology gives the elopement road two incompatible descriptions from the two people with a stake in it, so the paalai landscape is a speaker's argument, made terrible by the one who loses the girl and beautiful by the one who takes her.

links.note: Kuttuvan's land is the measure of wealth in both: in Purananuru 343 a father refuses wealth like Kuttuvan's Musiri as bride-price; in Akananuru 91 the man would not stay for Kuttuvan's Kudanadu, forgetting his wife.
links.teaches: Kuttuvan's riches stood in both books as the outer limit of wealth, and both poems use it to say a woman outweighs it: in puram the father refuses it for his daughter, in akam the husband refuses it for his wife.

links.note: Purananuru 39 praises the Chola assembly at Uraiyur where justice stands unfailing; Akananuru 93 compares the man's hard-won treasure to the virtue-filled assembly of the Cholas at Uraiyur.
links.teaches: The justice of Uraiyur's assembly, a praise theme in puram, was famous enough to serve an akam poet as a simile for something precious, so the court's moral fame had become a byword for worth itself.

links.note: Kural 524 says the fruit of gaining wealth is to be surrounded by kin; the man in 93 gives exactly this reason (ending the kin's ruin, feeding relatives, making strangers kin) for the journey that took him from his wife.
links.teaches: The Kural's purpose for wealth is the very reason the paalai hero gives for leaving, so the akam poem shows what the maxim costs in separation, and puts the return to the wife, not the kin, at the end.

links.note: In Kural 1147 the woman says the town's gossip manures her love-sickness and her mother's words water it; in Akananuru 95 the mother answers the gossiping women in her daughter's defence, and that trust is what the girl cannot face.
links.teaches: The Kural's couplet assumes a scolding mother whose words feed the love; the Sangam scene shows the harder case, where the mother's kindness against the town's gossip is what leaves the girl helpless, so the same two pressures can work through trust as well as blame.

links.note: Thirumurugatruppadai lists the velan's veriyattu ground (வேலன் தைஇய வெறியயர் களனும்) among the true places where Murugan comes to those who seek him; in Akananuru 98 the same rite, with kadambu, palm leaf and the god's great name praised, is a misreading of love-sickness by deluded women.
links.teaches: The same veriyattu rite is a real dwelling of the god in the devotional idyll and a comic error in the love poem, so the Sangam akam convention could treat Murugan's possession as a cover story without denying the god, who here might even cure her.

source_issues: 81: the base text numbers the last line 13 though the poem has 15 lines (flagged); a misprinted number.
84 line 12: அரிஞ்ர் is not a word; read அரிநர் (reapers), the word the sense needs.
86 line 31: மா அ யோளே is split by stray spaces; read மாஅயோளே.
89 lines 7 to 8 (காழியர் கவ்வைப் பரப்பின் வெவ்வுவர்ப்பு ஒழிய): rare words whose sense is not secure; the reading of the poem does not turn on them.
90 line 14: பாசிலை விலையே is obscure (a green-leaf courtship gift, or the girl's worth); the verse is marked uncertain.
93 line 17: a stray space before the comma (கடாஅத்து ,).
95: the colophon reads போக்குடன் பட்ட தலைமகன் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது, but the speaker is the woman (என் தளிர்புரை மேனி; the mother says என் மகட்கு of her); read தலைமகள்.
96 line 7: வீஞ்குபு is not a word; read வீங்குபு (swelling).
97: the colophon's வற்புறுந்துந் is a misprint for வற்புறுத்தும்.
98 line 22: பெண்டிற்க்கு is misspelt for பெண்டிர்க்கு.
99: the colophon thurai ends with a comma instead of a full stop.
85 line 2, 92 line 2 and 96 line 18 recur in 147, 108 and 368 (flagged): formulaic lines, not errors.
